Work Place Safety - Evacuation Chairs & Stretchers
Headings marked [H2] should be set as H2 on the page.
[H2] Evacuation Chairs for Stairs, Evacuation Sleds, and Rescue Stretchers

moves a person who cannot walk down the stairs safely when the elevators are out of service, during a fire, power outage, earthquake, or medical emergency. Anchortex carries Evac+Chair stair evacuation chairs, powered stair climbing chairs, evacuation sleds, and accessories, along with Rapid Extraction (REX) rescue stretchers, for hospitals, nursing homes, schools, offices, high-rise buildings, and correctional facilities.

Most evac chair models are operated by one person: the passenger sits in a secure seat while the operator guides the chair down the stairs on tracks or belts that control the speed. Some models also carry a passenger up the stairs. An evacuation chair can be used in place of an evacuation wheelchair on stairs, where a standard wheelchair cannot go.

Evac+Chair 300H, 400H, 600H, and 750H stair evacuation chairs for controlled travel down the stairs, with weight capacities from 400 to 500 lbs. The 600H and 750H also have extra handles so two people can carry a passenger up the stairs.
The battery powered Evac+Chair Power 800 and Power 900 carry a passenger up or down the stairs with one operator, for emergency evacuation and daily patient transport.
The IBEX 700H Tran-Seat lets two people move a patient up and down the stairs without carrying or heavy lifting.
The Evac+Sled, the Ulti-Mat (standard and bariatric sizes), and the Evac+Sheet rescue sheet, which stays under the mattress, for moving people who cannot sit, or bedridden patients, down the stairs.
REX ONE, REX DCS with descent control for stairs and steep ground, and REX DCS/CF for correctional facilities. Each folds in three for storage and lets one responder move a patient.
Comfy Seat cushions, the Transporter seat for transfers from a wheelchair, metal storage cabinets, anti-theft alarms, and the iEvac smoke and fire escape hood.
[H2] How to Choose an Evacuation Chair
Check the rated capacity against the people who may need it. The 750H is rated to 500 lbs, and the Ulti-Mat comes in a bariatric size
Most models need one trained operator; some need two, and some allow two-person carrying when needed
Manual evacuation chairs are made for going down the stairs. For going up, choose a powered stair chair, the IBEX 700H, or a model with carry handles
Measure the stair landings and plan where each chair will be kept. Wall mounting and storage cabinets keep chairs close to the stairs and ready to use
Train staff on the chair, practice regularly, and include it in the building's emergency action plan
A lightweight, folding stair chair that lets one or two operators move a person with limited mobility down the stairs, and with some models up the stairs, during an emergency.
How many people does it take to operate an evac chair?
Most manual Evac+Chair models and the powered Power 800 and Power 900 need one operator. The IBEX 700H needs two. Models with carry handles can be lifted by two people.
Can an evacuation chair go up the stairs?
Yes, with the right model. The powered Power 800 and Power 900 and the IBEX 700H go up and down the stairs. The 600H and 750H can be carried up by two people.
Where should evacuation chairs be kept?
Near the stairways, on a wall mount or in a storage cabinet, so staff can reach them quickly.

Evac+Chair has made stairway evacuation chairs since 1982, and its chairs were designed in the United States. Rapid Extraction designs and builds REX rescue stretchers in the U.S.A. Explore the full line of

Shop evacuation chairs for stairs from Evac+Chair, plus evacuation sleds and REX rescue stretchers for safe emergency evacuation of mobility impaired people.

Anchortex's Evacuation Chairs & Stretchers are designed for safe patient transport during emergencies, including mobility‑assisted evacuation solutions for hospitals and other facilities. Shop Anchortex!

Keywords: this page uses Ricky's primary keyword "evacuation chair" in the H1 area, the first sentence, a heading and the FAQs, and the secondary keywords evac chair, evacuation chairs for stairs, emergency evacuation chair, stair evacuation chair, evacuation wheelchair, evacuation sled, and rescue stretcher. "Emergency stair chair" (90) and "rescue chair" (50) are not used yet; tell me if you want them worked in.

H1: the collection title is "Work Place Safety - Evacuation Chairs & Stretchers". I suggest "Evacuation Chairs and Rescue Stretchers". If "Work Place Safety -" is needed for your menus or other collections, we can keep it in the title and change only the SEO title.

Evacuation wheelchair: Andrew suggested "The REX chair can be used instead of an evacuation wheelchair in some circumstances." REX is a stretcher, so I wrote it about evacuation chairs ("An evacuation chair can be used in place of an evacuation wheelchair on stairs, where a standard wheelchair cannot go"). Please check this is what you meant.

Evac-Chair brand focuses on making chairs that help move disabled people down stairs in a emergency, when elevators are not available.  REC stretchers are used for somewhat similar situations but are not meant for going down stairs.

Capacities: I used only what our product pages say: 300H 400 lbs, 400H 440 lbs, 750H 500 lbs. The Power 900 page says 560 lbs, but the Evac+Chair website says "up to 500lbs", so I left powered chair capacities out of this page.

Power 400H: our product name says "Power 400H", but the Evac+Chair website lists the 400H as a manual chair (440 lbs), and our page describes it for downward evacuation. I listed it with the manual chairs. Is the 400H powered?
Names: the Evac+Chair website does not use "Power 1-800" (it says Power 800), "Transporter", "Evac+Alarm", or "Rescue Sheet" (it says Evac+Sheet). I used the website names on this page.
REX DCS/CF: the Rapid Extraction website lists only REX ONE and REX DCS. The CF (correctional facility) version is described on our product page only.
FAQs: I added four short FAQs, because buyers search these questions and the Evac+Chair website answers them. Tell me if you want them on the collection page or left out.
Links: there is an Evac+Chair collection, but no Rapid Extraction collection, so I linked only to Evac+Chair.
REX DCS/CF: Rapid Extraction Correctional Facility Stretcher

Primary: correctional facility stretcher (0/mo). Support only: rescue stretcher (200), rescue litter (150). Jail, inmate, and prison stretcher all show 0. Ricky's note: no search demand for correctional terms, write for the buyer; low volume, high value product (orders around $12K).
Rapid Extraction Correctional Facility Stretcher with Restraints – REX DCS/CF
REX DCS/CF – Multi-Purpose Extraction Stretcher for Correctional Facilities
Folding Rescue Stretcher with Humane Restraints and Stair Descent Control for Jail and Prison Response Teams
Rapid Extraction Rex DCS/CF Patient Evacuation Stretcher for Corrections and Detention Facilities
Headings marked [H2] should be set as H2 on the page.

is a correctional facility stretcher for jail and prison emergency response teams. It combines a folding rescue stretcher with built-in restraints and a descent control brake, so one officer can move an injured, ill, or restrained inmate across the facility, down the stairs, or out of the building in an emergency.

The tri-fold aluminum frame stores in a small space, is ready to roll in under 30 seconds, and has no components that can become weapons. Humane Restraint ankle and wrist cuffs attach to the frame, and pre-installed straps hold the chest, waist, and legs, so staff can move a restrained person safely and humanely with fewer officers.
Rugged T-6 aerospace aluminum with a tri-fold panel system
Ready to roll in under 30 seconds
Converts to a backboard, mobile stretcher, or patient treatment cot, and adjusts for supine and Fowler’s positions
Humane Restraint ankle and wrist cuffs that secure to the frame, plus pre-installed quick-release polypropylene chest, waist, and leg straps for full body restraint in incline and supine positions
Hand brake for controlled descent down stairs and steep ground; the parking brake keeps an unattended inmate from moving the stretcher; dual braking rods with an emergency auto-lock
Puncture-proof airless all-terrain tires on quick-release wheels
Flip-up headrest, adjustable pull handle, protective fenders, and front and rear kickstands
Designed and built in the USA
The REX DCS/CF suits jails, prisons, and detention centers that need to move inmates safely with fewer staff, whether the person is injured, ill, or resisting.
Restrain and move an inmate out of a cell and through the facility
Move injured inmates or officers to a point of care, from recreation injuries to mass-casualty incidents
Simple, low-profile patient loading and transport within the infirmary
Bring inmates down the stairs of multi-level buildings during a fire or other emergency
One officer can do work that would otherwise take several, freeing staff for other duties
Prison and Detention Hardware and Equipment
collections for more evacuation and restraint equipment.
Can one officer move a restrained inmate on the REX DCS/CF?
Yes. Once the inmate is restrained on the stretcher, a single officer can roll the REX DCS/CF through the facility and, with the descent control brake, down the stairs.
How is the REX DCS/CF different from the REX DCS?
The REX DCS/CF adds Humane Restraint ankle and wrist cuffs and pre-installed chest, waist, and leg straps for full body restraint, for use in correctional and detention facilities.
Can it be left with an inmate on board?
The parking brake keeps a restrained inmate from moving the stretcher by shifting their body weight. Follow your facility's policy for observing restrained inmates.
REX stretchers fold in three for compact storage and roll on airless all-terrain wheels, so one responder can move a patient over stairs, rough ground, and long distances.
Multi-purpose extraction stretcher that converts to a backboard, mobile stretcher, or treatment cot
The REX ONE with a Descent Control System hand brake for stairs and steep ground
The REX DCS for correctional facilities, with Humane Restraint cuffs and full body restraint straps
Rapid Extraction (REX EMS, LLC) of Glendora, California, designs and builds REX stretchers in the U.S.A., and REX stretchers won an EMS World Innovation Award.
REX DCS/CF Correctional Facility Stretcher at Anchortex
REX DCS/CF Multi-Purpose Extraction Stretcher for Corrections Facilities | Anchortex
Shop the REX DCS/CF correctional facility stretcher, a folding rescue stretcher with Humane Restraint cuffs and stair descent control for jail response teams.

Rapid Extraction REX extraction stretchers are a multi-functional, collapsible, all terrain stretcher designed to move the injured over varied terrain and conditions, faster and easier than ever before. Government and GSA pricing available.

Keywords: Ricky's primary keyword "correctional facility stretcher" is in the H1, the first sentence, the meta title, and the meta description. "Rescue stretcher" is used as support (subtitle, intro, meta description) and "rescue litter" is left for the REX DCS page, as Ricky noted. Jail, inmate, and prison are used as buyer language, since nobody searches the product terms.
Duplicate content: our current description is word for word the same as the American Detention Supplies page for this product. The new copy is fully rewritten, so the page is unique.

Specs: I used the REX for Correctional Facilities brochure (linked on the current page): 48 lbs, 400 lb load, 75”×26” open, 25”×18” folded. Our current page says "75”x18” fully assembled" and "less than 50 lbs." The REX website gives 42 lbs for the standard REX DCS, so the CF restraints add weight.
Shipping weight: all 4 variants are set to 75 lbs, but the stretcher weighs 48 lbs. Is 75 lbs the boxed weight with the carry case? Should we keep it?
Price: the 4 variants are $3,275 with no compare-at price. American Detention Supplies lists it at $3,285. No change made.
Current meta description says "Government and GSA pricing available." Is that still true? If so, should it go in the description (for example under Includes or in the intro)?
Ricky noted orders are around $12K, so buyers often order several units. Would you like a line such as "Contact us for quantity pricing"?
Brochure: the current page links a 2-page brochure PDF. I listed it as the spec sheet above. Do you want the download link kept on the page?
Colors: the brochure says custom colors are available. I left that out, as with other brands, because we sell the 4 standard colors.
Left out: the US patent number and "6 ft social distance" claim from the brochure.

FAQs: the competitor pages (American Detention Supplies, Bound Tree) have no FAQs. I added three short ones based on what buyers ask: one-officer use, how the CF differs from the REX DCS, and the parking brake.
Images: the 7 current images are kept. Their file names say "REX One Restraint Chair"; I did not rename them. All have alt text equal to the old product title.
